cards.front: Recall a key point about The League of Nations
cards.back: The League of Nations was created as part of the Treaty of Versailles in June 1919. It was Woodrow Wilson's idea - his Fourteenth Point called for "a general association of nations." The League's headquarters were in Geneva, Switzerland. Its first meeting was held on 15 November 1920 with 42 member states.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The League of Nations
cards.back: The League's Covenant (its founding document) set out its key principles: collective security, arbitration of disputes, disarmament, and improved living and working conditions worldwide. Article 10 of the Covenant committed all members to "respect and preserve" each other's territorial integrity.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The League of Nations
cards.back: The Council was the most powerful body. It had permanent members (Britain, France, Italy, Japan) who could veto decisions. However, ALL Council decisions had to be UNANIMOUS - any member could veto action. This meant the League was often paralysed by disagreement. A single "no" vote could prevent the League from acting against an aggressor.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The League of Nations
cards.back: The League's membership was fundamentally flawed from the start. The USA never joined; Germany was excluded until 1926; the USSR was excluded until 1934; and Japan and Italy left in the 1930s. No organisation can maintain world peace without the world's most powerful nations.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The League of Nations
cards.back: The League was more successful in the 1920s than is often remembered. It resolved several international disputes peacefully and carried out important humanitarian work. The problems of the 1930s should not overshadow the genuine achievements of the 1920s.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The League of Nations
cards.back: Fridtjof Nansen, the League's High Commissioner for Refugees, won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1922 for his work. The "Nansen Passport" he created provided identity documents for stateless refugees and was recognised by over 50 countries. The ILO won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1969 for its decades of work improving labour conditions.

cards.front: What should you know about history exam tips — the league of nations?
cards.back: 1. For The League of Nations, include specific factual detail: dates, names, events and statistics where relevant 2. For source questions, analyse provenance (who, when, why, audience) before using the content 3. In evaluation questions, discuss multiple factors and weigh their relative significance 4. Always link back to the question focus — don't just narrate what happened with The League of Nations 5. Use phrases like 'the most significant factor was... because...' to show analytical judgement

cards.front: What does Permanent Court of International Justice mean?
cards.back: 15 judges from different nations (e.g. Settled legal disputes between nations; gave advisory opinions)
Permanent officials (e.g. Administrative work; prepared reports; organised meetings)

cards.front: What does International Labour Organisation (ILO) mean?
cards.back: Government, employer, and worker representatives (e.g. Improved working conditions worldwide; set international labour standards)
NEVER joined (Senate rejected Treaty of Versailles) (e.g. World's strongest economy; most powerful military; absence destroyed League credibility)
Excluded 1919-1926; left 1933 (e.g. Europe's largest economy; key to European peace; exclusion was a deliberate humiliation)
